findings.claim: launchCloudDelete's catch-all clears the tombstone, and the tombstone is the only thing suppressing the cloud copy in refresh()'s merge. The round-2 supervisor ruling accepted 'orphan-doc risk'; what the code actually delivers is an undeletable drop that reappears in the user's own library on the next refresh, forever.
findings.evidence: The generic catch does `self?.clearPendingDelete(id)` and logs (DropStore.swift:390-398), on the stated rationale that a rules-denied delete 'must not read as a sync failure'. But refresh()'s merge skips a cloud row only while the tombstone lives: `if pendingDeleteIDs.contains(drop.id) { continue }` (DropStore.swift:234). Once cleared, the next `cloud.loadDrops` — a plain `whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)` query (FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-34) that still returns the undeleted document — falls through to `merged[drop.id] = drop` (DropStore.swift:235). The user's re-delete runs the identical path (local delete is a harmless no-op, tombstone set, denial, tombstone cleared), so the cycle is closed with no exit. There is no retry ceiling, no dead-letter set, and no user-visible signal — the failure is logged only.
findings.failureScenario: A deployment where the Firestore rules grant read/create/update but not delete on drops/{id} (precisely the README-step-5 misconfiguration class PBS-4 describes). The user deletes a synced drop from the Sent tab. It disappears, then reappears the next time anything calls refresh — the Explore tab's .task, the Sent toolbar button, or the auth-ready task on the next launch. Delete again: same. The drop is permanently undeletable from a UI that offers exactly one delete affordance, and the log line the developer would need is invisible on device. Worse, once it is back in `drops`, any AR slider commit on it calls library.update → local.save (DropStore.swift:277), writing the drop the user deleted back onto disk permanently.
findings.proposedFix: Distinguish 'the document is gone / was never there' from 'the delete was refused'. On a refused delete, keep the tombstone (so refresh keeps suppressing the row) and stop retrying it per-reconcile by moving it to a durable `unresolvedDeleteIDs` set that refresh() also honours; surface it once via lastSyncError or a dedicated banner rather than swallowing it. Only clear the tombstone on a confirmed delete, or on a NOT_FOUND-class error where the document provably does not exist.

findings.claim: A pending-sync id whose drop is not in the in-memory array is immortal: reconcileCloud only ever pushes ids it can find, and `remove()` is documented as the sole clearer — so an id for a drop that can no longer be loaded is never pushed, never cleared, and never expires. The pending set is persisted to UserDefaults, so the stuck state survives every relaunch.
findings.evidence: `for id in pendingSyncIDs where syncTasks[id] == nil { if let drop = drops.first(where: { $0.id == id }) { enqueueCloudSync(drop) } }` (DropStore.swift:319-323) — there is deliberately no else-branch (the C1/C10/C21 fix), and the doc comment states `remove()` is the sole legitimate clearer (DropStore.swift:312-316). The set is rehydrated at init from UserDefaults (DropStore.swift:211-212) and re-persisted on every mutation (DropStore.swift:413-417). But a drop can leave `drops` permanently without ever passing through remove(): the resilient decode skips a type-mismatched or id-less row (DropStore.swift:91-97), and the whole-file quarantine moves every row away (DropStore.swift:111). ProfileScreen's status branch checks `!library.pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty` before it will ever render 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops', and ShareDropSheet.swift:135 gates its 'Still uploading' copy on the same set.
findings.failureScenario: User creates a drop on the subway with no connectivity. add() persists it and marks it pending; pendingSyncDropIDs is written to UserDefaults. Before the upload lands, drops.json is damaged (or a newer build wrote one type-mismatched field into that drop's row). On the next launch the resilient decode skips that row — correct behaviour, and the transient 'saved drops couldn't be read' banner appears once. But the pending id survives in UserDefaults with nothing to match it. From then on, on every launch forever, Profile reads 'Uploading 1 drop…' instead of 'Synced', and if the user ever opens the share sheet for any drop while the counter is non-zero the sync chip contradicts itself. Where the load was not clean, keep the id but stop counting it as 'uploading': track it in a separate `unresolvedSyncIDs` set that Profile reports as a problem ('1 drop couldn't be uploaded') rather than as progress. Either way the pending counter must be bounded by what the library can actually push.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified in the source: DropStore.swift:368-373 clears pending and records the terminal outcome only in a single global `lastSyncError`, which line 237 nils on any successful cloud read and line 365 nils on any other drop's ack, and the failure precondition is documented platform behavior (Firebase Auth stores its token with `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`, and `ThisDeviceOnly` items provably do not migrate on device restore, so a restored drops.json carries an ownerUid no live UID can match).
solutions.industrialSolution: Three layers, in order of leverage. (1) REPRESENTATION: stop storing per-record outcomes in shared UI slots. The industry standard is the transactional outbox — each record carries its own durable sync state written in the SAME transaction as the record: `syncState ∈ {clean, pendingUpload, inFlight(since:), failedRetryable(attempts, nextAttemptAt), failedTerminal(reason)}` plus `updatedAt` and `lastError`. "Synced" then becomes a COMPUTATION (`rows.allSatisfy { $0.syncState == .clean }`), not a mutable string, so no other drop's success can clobber it and no read can erase it. On Apple platforms this means Core Data/SwiftData or SQLite (GRDB), not `drops.json` + `Set<UUID>` in UserDefaults — two stores that cannot be written atomically, which is the structural root. (2) CLASSIFICATION: map `FirestoreErrorCode` to permanence at one site — `.permissionDenied`/`.unauthenticated` = terminal-needs-user-action, `.unavailable`/`.deadlineExceeded`/`.aborted`/`.resourceExhausted` = retryable with backoff, `.notFound` = already resolved. The app currently collapses this taxonomy into a `String?`. (3) ROOT CAUSE: the terminal error should be unreachable, not merely visible. `ownerUid` is server-owned identity and must never be persisted into the local model — set it only inside the `CloudDrop` write wrapper and enforce it server-side (`request.resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid`), so a UID change makes the local copy re-uploadable rather than permanently orphaned. For identity continuity, Firebase's documented mechanism is anonymous→permanent upgrade via `link(with:)` credential linking (which also exempts the account from anonymous auto-cleanup); production apps prompt for this at the first moment the user creates content worth losing. Where documents genuinely exist under a dead UID, the standard remedy is a server-side re-parenting step (callable Cloud Function that reassigns `ownerUid` after verifying the client holds the old token), never a client-side retry. Apple's CloudKit avoids the whole class because the record zone is bound to the iCloud account rather than a client-minted id.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — DropStore.swift:84-87 unconditionally nils `pendingReadWarning` when the file is absent, the quarantine branch at 108-114 has just made it absent, and three refresh triggers fire within ~1s of launch (AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:34, RootView.swift:121-124, MapScreen.swift:105-107); the C7 test asserts the warning after exactly one load and even asserts the self-healing behavior as correct, so it structurally cannot catch this.
solutions.industrialSolution: Distinguish LEVELS from EVENTS. A destructive outcome ("your library was unreadable and has been quarantined") is an incident that must be journaled durably and cleared only by explicit acknowledgement — never a level recomputed from the most recent read, because the recovery action itself erases the evidence. Industrial shape: write a durable quarantine manifest at the moment of destruction — `{quarantineFilename, timestamp, byteCount, rowsLost, acknowledged: false}` — as a sibling file or a UserDefaults record, and have the library publish it until the user dismisses it. `loadDrops` must never treat "file absent" as evidence of health; absent is `unknown`, not `clean`. Apple's HIG is explicit that irreversible/destructive outcomes require acknowledgement rather than a transient notice. The deeper industrial fix is that this branch should be unreachable: hand-rolled JSON blobs have no crash-safe write path for external corruption, whereas SQLite (WAL journaling) and Core Data/SwiftData make "the entire store is unparseable" effectively unreachable from a partial write, and give you row-level recovery instead of all-or-nothing quarantine. Also add a rotating backup (write N-1 aside before each persist) so quarantine has a restore path rather than only a forensic sidecar, and separate `FileProtectionType`/data-protection read failures (readable only after first unlock) from genuine corruption — they are different incidents with different remedies.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and its sharpest sub-claim is the most important one in the whole review: `let data = try Data(contentsOf: fileURL)` at DropStore.swift:88 sits outside the do/catch so a read throw leaves `pendingReadWarning` stale, refresh swallows it with `try?` at :219, the anti-rollback guard at :233 fails its `merged[drop.id] != nil` condition when local truth is empty, and — verified — there is no timestamp or version comparison anywhere in the merge.
solutions.industrialSolution: Two industrial rules, both violated here. (1) A sync pass that cannot read local truth must ABORT, not proceed — this is basic replication discipline (a replica that cannot read its own log does not apply remote writes). Replace `try?` with a do/catch that records a distinct `localReadError`, and skip the merge and the `drops =` publish entirely. `try?` is designed for "failure is uninteresting", which is never true at the primary datastore boundary. (2) Merges need a conflict rule, and the industry-standard minimum is last-writer-wins on an explicit version: Firestore's canonical shape is a server-authoritative `updatedAt` written with `FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` plus a monotonic client revision counter, compared on merge. Apple's own equivalent, NSPersistentCloudKitContainer, defaults to LWW on CloudKit `modifiedAt` and exposes `NSMergePolicy.mergeByPropertyObjectTrump` for the property-level variant — either is a documented, shipped answer, and both beat the current "cloud row unconditionally wins unless a flag happens to be set". For stronger guarantees the reference is version vectors / CRDTs (Kleppmann, DDIA ch. 5). Separately, `reconcileCloud` re-reading the pending drop from the post-merge in-memory array is a read-your-own-writes violation; every production outbox re-reads the row from the store inside the same transaction that marks it in-flight, so it can never push a payload the read path just installed. That is also the third argument for making the outbox entry carry its own payload (see flows-5).

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED (and independently found by two other reviewers as concurrency-4 and flows-1, which is strong corroboration) — `merged` is built before both awaits and assigned wholesale at DropStore.swift:244 with no epoch check, while `add`/`remove` mutate `drops` from the same @MainActor during those suspensions; one precision note, this is a high-level lost-update race, not a data race, because actor isolation deliberately does not prevent reentrancy.
solutions.industrialSolution: Apple documents this exact hazard: actors are reentrant, and the stated rule from WWDC 2021's "Protect mutable state with Swift actors" is to re-check your assumptions after every `await` because state can change across a suspension. The three standard remedies, in ascending order of quality: (a) an epoch/generation token captured at entry and re-checked before every publish — the same discipline the wave already applied to the write pipeline and simply never applied to the read path; (b) single-flight the operation (`if let inFlight = refreshTask { return await inFlight.value }`) so two refreshes cannot exist; (c) the actually correct fix — stop replacing the array. The industrial shape for a remote-backed collection is to apply DIFFS to the current state, never to overwrite it with a pre-await snapshot. For Firestore specifically this is a first-class documented API: `addSnapshotListener` delivers `snapshot.documentChanges` as `.added/.modified/.removed`, so the store applies deltas to live state and a concurrent local delete simply cannot be undone by an in-flight read. That also deletes the three imperative refresh triggers — one listener whose lifetime is bound to auth. Architecturally this is unidirectional data flow: the network response is an ACTION reduced into current state (Flux/Redux/TCA; Apple's own analogue is NSFetchedResultsController and `NSPersistentStoreRemoteChange` notifications, where the store is truth and views observe diffs). Finally, apply `pendingDeleteIDs` as a filter over the WHOLE merged set immediately before publishing, not just over the cloud loop — a tombstoned id must be unpublishable from any source.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — `lastPersistError` is a single global slot nil'd on success at DropStore.swift:259, :282 and :296, `remove()` throws before mutating `drops` so the failed row re-renders, and the loop at DropsListScreen.swift:92-98 discards every error with `try?`; the code comment claiming failures surface via the banner is false for any non-final failure in the batch.
solutions.industrialSolution: Batch operations must either be transactional or report per-item outcomes — there is no third option, and Apple ships the canonical shape for the second: CloudKit's `CKModifyRecordsOperation` reports `perRecordSaveBlock`/`perRecordDeleteBlock` per item and surfaces aggregate failure as `CKError.partialFailure` with `partialErrorsByItemID`, precisely so one item's success cannot mask another's failure. Mirror that: the delete API returns `[(UUID, Result<Void, Error>)]`, the call site aggregates into one honest summary ("2 of 3 drops couldn't be deleted"), and per-row state lives on the row (see sync-1's per-record state). Replace `lastPersistError: String?` with either that per-record state or an ordered `[FailureRecord]` that only the owning record's next success may clear. For the SwiftUI list specifically, the standard optimistic-with-rollback pattern is: animate the removal, and on failure re-insert the row with an explicit alert explaining why — never silently re-render it back in, which reads to the user as a phantom. And never use `try?` inside a loop over user-initiated operations; that is the single most reliable source of this defect class across iOS codebases.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED as a defect (it is sync-1 reached by a second route), but one of its two stated triggers is OVERSTATED: a foreground launch cannot precede first unlock, since the user must unlock the device to tap the icon and `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` is readable thereafter — the unconditional trigger is device restore/new device, because `ThisDeviceOnly` keychain items provably do not migrate, and pre-first-unlock BACKGROUND launches (location/BGTask) are a real but much narrower path.
solutions.industrialSolution: Same representation fix as sync-1 — durable per-record `failedTerminal(reason)` state that outranks "Synced" in every surface — plus two additions this finding specifically motivates. (1) Never let a UID transition silently invalidate local data. The industrial pattern is an explicit identity-migration step: on `Auth.addStateDidChangeListener` observing a UID change, run a one-time reconciliation that either re-parents documents server-side (callable Cloud Function verifying the old token) or, for never-uploaded rows, rewrites `ownerUid = nil` locally and re-enqueues — and if neither is possible, records a durable terminal state the user is told about. Firebase's documented long-term answer is to stop the UID being ephemeral at all via anonymous→permanent linking. (2) The app needs exactly one authoritative "is my data safe?" surface, computed by reducing over per-record states rather than assembled from independent mutable strings. Firestore even supplies the primitive for the transient half: `Firestore.waitForPendingWrites()` and per-document `snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites` are the documented signals for "the server has it", which the app currently re-implements incorrectly with `pendingSyncIDs`. Also worth noting for triage: Identity Platform's anonymous-account auto-cleanup (30 days) is opt-in, so that premise is conditional — the restore premise is not.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED on the lost-update core — verified there is no in-flight flag, no re-check of `profile == nil` before `setDataAcked` or before `profile = starter`, and `merge: true` means a late attempt 2 genuinely overwrites a user edit that landed during the 1.5s backoff; the "grows without bound" fan-out variant is OVERSTATED (each loop is bounded at 3 attempts and each snapshot event spawns at most one loop, so growth is bounded by event rate, not unbounded) though the repeated-write effect is real.
solutions.industrialSolution: "Create iff absent" is not a client-side problem and should not be solved with client retries. In order of industrial preference: (1) Seed server-side — a Firebase Auth blocking function (`beforeUserCreated`) or an Auth `onCreate` Cloud Function writes `users/{uid}` once, atomically, before the client ever observes the account. This is Google's documented pattern for profile bootstrapping and eliminates the race, the retry loop, the rules exposure, and the seed-vs-edit conflict simultaneously. (2) If it must stay client-side, make it atomic on the server: `runTransaction` that reads the doc and writes only when absent, or enforce create-only semantics in rules (`allow create: if !exists(...)`) so a late seed is REJECTED rather than merged — and treat `alreadyExists` as success. (3) Never use `merge: true` for a seed. Merge is exactly the operator that lets a stale starter payload overwrite live fields; a seed is a create, and its failure is the signal that seeding was unnecessary. On the Swift side, single-flight is the standard idiom: hold `private var seedTask: Task<Void, Never>?`, set it synchronously before any `await` (safe on @MainActor), and have subsequent callers `await` the existing task instead of starting a new one — task memoization, the same pattern used for image/asset caches. Re-check `guard profile == nil else { return }` immediately before the write and again before assigning, since Apple's actor-reentrancy guidance requires re-validating preconditions after every suspension. Finally, `seedProfile` and `updateProfile` writing the same document concurrently is a textbook lost update; the documented remedy is a transaction, or `updateData` restricted to the fields that path owns.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified `performCloudSync` does not check generation or cancellation until line 363, AFTER `cloud.save`, and the Firestore continuation at FirebaseDropStore.swift:76-90 has no cancellation handler; the offline non-invocation of the completion is documented behavior (firebase-ios-sdk #3303/#478: the completion fires only on server commit), and the ~1 sustained write/sec per-document limit is documented — one correction, `withTaskCancellationHandler` would free the Swift-side continuation but CANNOT un-queue a mutation already handed to Firestore, so it does not prevent the stale writes.
solutions.industrialSolution: The entry guard is right and cheap — `guard !Task.isCancelled, syncGenerations[drop.id] == generation else { return }` as the first statement, matching Apple's documented cooperative-cancellation contract (check at entry and at every suspension point; a cancelled task's body still runs). But the real fix is to never enqueue 40 writes. The industry-standard control is COALESCING at the source: a trailing debounce on the commit (200–500 ms after slider release) plus strict one-in-flight-per-document with a `needsRepush` dirty flag — when a write is already in flight, set the flag instead of stacking a task, and issue exactly one follow-up write of the CURRENT state when it completes. This is the `conflate`/`debounce` operator that every reactive stack ships (Combine `.debounce`, swift-async-algorithms `.debounce`/`.throttle`, Kotlin Flow `conflate`), and it is what keeps you under Firestore's documented 1 write/sec/document soft limit — exceeding it sustained produces exactly the latency and `aborted` contention errors described. Second: stop duplicating Firestore's own outbox. Firestore already persists its mutation queue to disk and replays it across launches; writing the same document 40 times offline is the app's choice, not the SDK's requirement. Write final state on commit, and answer "is it up?" with `metadata.hasPendingWrites` or `waitForPendingWrites()` rather than a hand-rolled parallel `pendingSyncIDs`. Third: if you keep the continuation bridge, `withTaskCancellationHandler` is still worth adding so cancelled tasks release their `GeoDrop` copy and continuation promptly — just do not expect it to prevent the network write.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED as the same defect as sync-4/flows-1, verified at DropStore.swift:217-246 with both refresh triggers confirmed (AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:34 pre-auth, RootView.swift:121-124 on `.task(id: account.uid ?? "-")`); the specific create-wizard collision window is narrow so MEDIUM is fair, but the underlying clobber is hit far more often by the tab-switch and GPS-fix triggers than by this scenario.
solutions.industrialSolution: Identical to sync-4 and it should be fixed once, not three times: epoch guard after every await, single-flight the refresh, and — the durable fix — apply diffs from `addSnapshotListener`/`documentChanges` into live state instead of assigning a pre-await snapshot over `drops`. Two SwiftUI-specific points this finding raises correctly. First, `.task(id:)` is documented to cancel and restart when the id changes and to cancel on disappear, but that cancellation is cooperative — the Firestore `getDocuments()` bridge is not cancellation-aware, so the body resumes and runs to the assignment anyway; `guard !Task.isCancelled` after each await is therefore mandatory, not optional hygiene. Second, having three independent view-lifecycle triggers own the same global refresh is itself the architectural smell: data loading should be owned by the store and bound to the authentication/scene lifecycle once, with views observing published state — SwiftUI's `.task` is for view-scoped work, and using it as a global data-sync trigger from three screens guarantees overlap. Bind one listener to the auth state (`Auth.addStateDidChangeListener`), tear it down on sign-out, and delete the manual refresh calls entirely.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED and the cleanest finding in the set — verified DropStoreTests.swift setUp/tearDown mutate `UserDefaults.standard` using the literal shipping key `pendingSyncDropIDs` and never touch `pendingDeleteDropIDs`, and `makeLibrary` builds a real `DropLibrary` whose init reads both keys from `.standard`; the reviewer's line citations for the stub are wrong (the file is 253 lines, not 2000+) but every substantive claim checks out, and since this is a hosted iOS test target `UserDefaults.standard` is genuinely the app's domain.
solutions.industrialSolution: Dependency-inject the defaults — Apple ships the exact affordance: `UserDefaults(suiteName:)` creates an isolated domain, and `removePersistentDomain(forName:)` cleans it. Standard shape: `init(..., defaults: UserDefaults = .standard)`, tests pass `UserDefaults(suiteName: "DropLibraryTests-\(UUID().uuidString)")!` and tear down the whole domain, so no test can reach production state and no test can leak into the next. The general rule is that a test must never mutate global state it does not own — under swift-testing this is enforced with injected dependencies plus `@Suite(.serialized)` where shared resources are unavoidable. But the deeper signal here is architectural, and it is the same one as flows-5: sync bookkeeping does not belong in UserDefaults at all. `UserDefaults` is documented as a preferences store; it cannot be written atomically with drops.json, so the outbox and the entity store can always disagree — which is what makes an accidental key removal catastrophic rather than merely inconvenient. Moving both into one transactional store (Core Data/SwiftData/SQLite) makes this test smell disappear along with the class of bug it points at. Finally, CI should run on freshly erased simulators rather than developer devices, so a harness bug cannot destroy real user state.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and its most valuable claim is the one that explains the other findings: verified `StubCloudStore` is `@MainActor` (DropStoreTests.swift:236-253) with a `save` containing no `await`, so from `@MainActor DropLibrary` the call `try await cloud.save(drop)` never actually suspends, no main-actor interleaving is possible in any test, and the C2/C22 generation guards are structurally unexercised — which is exactly why concurrency-3's missing entry guard survived a green suite; one nuance, the SE-0338 citation is correct for Swift 5/6.0 mode but SE-0461 (Swift 6.2) changes the default so nonisolated async functions run on the caller's actor, which will alter these hop points during migration.
solutions.industrialSolution: The load-bearing rule is: a test double must reproduce the real implementation's ISOLATION and its SUSPENSION POINTS, otherwise it tests a program that does not exist. The industrial technique is a controllable gate — the fake holds a `CheckedContinuation` (or an `AsyncStream` handle) that the test resumes explicitly, so the test can park a write mid-flight, deterministically drive a second `enqueueCloudSync`/`remove`/`refresh` into the gap, and then release it. That turns "generation guards are correct" from an untestable assertion into a deterministic test, and it is how Apple's own async test samples and swift-testing's `confirmation` are structured. Make the fake an `actor` or a nonisolated final class with a lock — never `@MainActor` when production is not. For the seam itself, follow the Swift migration guide: declare `protocol DropStore: Sendable`, make `FirebaseDropStore` a stateless `final class ...: DropStore, Sendable`, and add a warning-only CI lane with `SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY = complete` now (the documented incremental path) before flipping `SWIFT_VERSION = 6.0`. Swift 6.2's `defaultIsolation = MainActor` (SE-0466) plus `nonisolated(nonsending)` (SE-0461) is the pragmatic landing zone for an app-shaped codebase like this and materially reduces the annotation burden.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified `preloadAnimatedAssets` fires `onAssetLoaded?(name, entity != nil)` into an optional handler installed only by `attach()`, the preload is scheduled 10s after `configure` (ARSessionHolder.swift:34-37) which on the dominant path precedes any camera intent, `failedAssets` is never cleared and is read only at DropEntityFactory.swift:134 and :218, and `animatedModel` returns `text("3D?")` forever with no user-facing message.
solutions.industrialSolution: Two corrections, one architectural and one process. ARCHITECTURAL: make asset state queryable at render time rather than announced at decode time. The canonical Apple shape is `AsyncImagePhase` — `.empty / .success(Image) / .failure(Error)` — a value the view reads whenever it renders, so a subscriber that arrives late still sees the truth. Mirror it: an observable `AssetRegistry` publishing `[String: AssetState]` where `AssetState = .loading | .ready(Entity) | .failed(Error)`; `animatedModel` reads it, and the session manager renders a sticky in-AR message for as long as any placed drop is showing the `3D?` marker. Any event channel that can fire before its subscriber exists needs replay semantics — Combine's `CurrentValueSubject`, a buffered `AsyncStream`, or the reconcile-on-attach pattern ARKit itself prescribes (on attach, scan existing state rather than relying on having heard the delivery callback). PROCESS — and this is the real fix: a corrupt bundled `.usdz` must never reach a user. Validate every asset in CI with `usdchecker` from the OpenUSD toolset, and add a build/test step that actually calls `Entity.load` on every bundled asset on the target OS, failing the build on error. Reality Composer Pro validates on import for the same reason. In-AR messaging is the fallback for field conditions, not the control for a shipping defect. Finally, classify decode failures: a permanent negative cache is right for a malformed file but wrong for a memory-pressure or thermal failure, which production loaders retry with backoff.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified ShareDropSheet.swift:130-146 is a three-way chain on `shareError` then `pendingSyncIDs.contains` then a reassuring default, `library.lastSyncError` is never referenced in the file, the terminal branch at DropStore.swift:368-373 clears exactly the flag the middle branch depends on, and `.sheet(isPresented:onDismiss: { dismiss() })` tears the sheet down as the activity view closes.
solutions.industrialSolution: The governing rule is: never hand out a URL to a resource that is not yet durable and reachable. Three industrial mechanisms, and the app should use all three. (1) GATE THE CTA on a real acknowledgement signal. Firestore documents two: per-document `snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites == false` (latency compensation means the local write is visible immediately, and the metadata flag is the documented way to tell local-only from server-confirmed) and `Firestore.waitForPendingWrites()` for the aggregate. Either is correct; `pendingSyncIDs` is a home-grown re-implementation that is wrong in exactly the terminal case. (2) DEFER THE ITEM, not the sheet. `UIActivityViewController` supports asynchronous item resolution via `UIActivityItemProvider`/`NSItemProvider`, so you can present the share UI immediately and produce the link only once the upload acks — or refuse and explain. (3) MAKE THE LINK DEGRADE GRACEFULLY. Route the magic link through a server-side universal-link handler so an unresolved drop yields "this drop is still being prepared" rather than "this drop isn't available"; since Firebase Dynamic Links has been shut down, a self-hosted universal link plus an App Store fallback page is the current industrial baseline anyway, and that page is the natural place for this state. On the code shape, extract the caption into a pure function returning an exhaustive `enum ShareState { saving, failedLocal(String), pendingUpload, failedTerminal(String), ready }` fed by per-record sync state — an exhaustive `switch` makes the compiler refuse to let a future state fall through to the reassuring default, which is the specific mechanism that would have prevented this regression.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified RootView.swift:56-61 fires `Task { try? await library.update(drop, persist: true) }` and then synchronously sets `router.showCamera = true`, `lastPersistError` is rendered in exactly one place (DropsListScreen.swift:44-48) which is behind the full-screen cover, `update` applies the in-memory mutation before the throwing disk write so the drop renders regardless, and MapScreen.swift:36 repeats the pattern on a screen with no banner at all.
solutions.industrialSolution: Two rules. (1) NEVER NAVIGATE ON AN UNAWAITED WRITE. The receive flow is a commit-then-transition step and must be written as one: `do { try await library.update(drop); router.showCamera = true } catch { present(error, retry:) }`. Losing a received gift because the save failed is a correctness bug, and iOS gives you a specific, distinguishable error for the dominant cause — `NSFileWriteOutOfSpaceError` — plus `volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsageKey` to check headroom before large writes and say something specific. (2) ERROR PRESENTATION MUST BE GLOBAL, NOT PER-SCREEN. The standard iOS architecture puts a single error surface at the root scene, fed by the store's error publisher, so no screen can be the only renderer and no full-screen cover can hide it: `.alert(isPresented:error:actions:message:)` on the root view, with domain errors conforming to `LocalizedError` so a generic presenter gets `errorDescription`, `failureReason` and `recoverySuggestion` — that protocol exists precisely to decouple who raises an error from who shows it. Apple's HIG requires telling people what happened and what they can do about it. Concretely for this codebase: render the persist-error surface once at `RootView` level as an overlay/alert (which also fixes MapScreen for free), and additionally push the message into the in-AR channel via `manager.showPersistError` for the camera-covered case, since a root alert cannot appear over a `fullScreenCover` in every configuration.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified `frameUpdate` returns at GeoARSessionManager.swift:2018-2019 on `isInterrupted`/`sessionFailed`/mode before ever reaching the farMode computation at ~2095-2108, the flag has no other write site, and `tick()`/`updatePowerTier` bail on the same conditions; the premise that RealityKit keeps rendering during an interruption matches Apple's documentation that `sessionWasInterrupted` means the SESSION stops processing frames and tracking, not that the renderer stops, so an installed post-process pass keeps costing a full-screen offscreen render.
solutions.industrialSolution: The general principle is: derive state where it is CONSUMED, and never write a derived flag inside a branch guarded by one of that flag's own inputs — that construction makes the flag undefined in exactly the states the guard excludes. Industrially this is the reconciler pattern: one pure `farModeDecision(sessionLive:semanticActive:thermalSerious:tier:anyHolderBeyond:)` and one `updateSemanticPass()` that computes desired state from current inputs and applies the delta, invoked from EVERY transition rather than from the render loop — structurally the same as SwiftUI's render function or UIKit's `setNeedsUpdateConfiguration`. ARKit gives you the exact transition hooks to call it from: `sessionWasInterrupted(_:)`, `sessionInterruptionEnded(_:)`, `session(_:didFailWithError:)` and `session(_:cameraDidChangeTrackingState:)`; Apple's session-lifecycle guidance is to hide or disable AR content on interruption and to `run(options: [.resetTracking, .removeExistingAnchors])` on resume. For the power half: detach rather than gate. An installed `arView.renderCallbacks.postProcess` costs an offscreen target and a blit for every rendered frame regardless of what the closure decides internally, so the correct action on interrupt/fail/suspend/detach is `renderCallbacks.postProcess = nil` plus `semanticFeed.setEnabled(false)` plus `semanticMatteArmed = false`, and the same on `ProcessInfo.thermalStateDidChangeNotification` reaching `.serious`. Consider also `session.pause()` while interrupted. And a HUD chip that claims a subsystem is armed must read the subsystem's actual state, not a cached flag — same class as every other finding here.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — third independent report of the DropStore.swift:244 wholesale-replace defect, and it adds the most accurate mechanism detail of the three: SwiftUI does cancel MapScreen's `.task` on tab switch (documented), but Swift cancellation is cooperative and the Firestore `getDocuments()` bridge never checks it, so the continuation resumes and the body runs on to the unconditional assignment regardless.
solutions.industrialSolution: Same fix as sync-4/concurrency-4, which is itself the point — three reviewers finding one line means it should be fixed once, structurally. Minimum viable: `refreshGeneration` captured at entry, `guard refreshGeneration == captured, !Task.isCancelled else { return }` after every await and before touching `drops`, `lastSyncError` or `localReadWarning`; and merge into the CURRENT `drops` rather than a pre-await snapshot. Correct: delete the imperative refresh entirely. Firestore's documented architecture for a synced collection is a single `addSnapshotListener` whose lifetime is bound to the auth state, delivering `snapshot.documentChanges` as `.added/.modified/.removed`, applied as deltas to a store that is the single owner of `drops`. That gives you real-time updates for free, removes all three competing `.task` triggers, removes the wholesale replace, and makes the deleted-during-read resurrection unrepresentable rather than merely guarded. Pair it with `metadata.hasPendingWrites` so local, unacknowledged edits are visibly distinct from server-confirmed ones — which is also the honest input for the share CTA in arui-2/flows-3. The general form of the lesson: any code that computes state from a snapshot and then publishes it after a suspension is a lost-update waiting to happen; publish diffs, or re-derive after the await, never both-neither.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — same defect as sync-2, verified identically, and it correctly folds in the second silent path (the `Data(contentsOf:)` throw at DropStore.swift:88 sitting outside the do/catch, swallowed again by `try?` at :219) that sync-3 analyses separately; the two-refresh launch sequence is confirmed in AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:34 and RootView.swift:121-124.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-2: journal the destructive event durably at the moment it happens and clear it only on explicit acknowledgement, never recompute it from the last load — 'the file vanished' is not evidence of health, and the quarantine action is what made it vanish. Persist a quarantine manifest (`{filename, timestamp, byteCount, acknowledged}`) that `loadDrops` never clears on a missing file, and OR it with the transient skipped-rows warning in `refresh`. Wrap `Data(contentsOf:)` so a read failure sets a distinct warning before propagating, and stop swallowing it with `try?`. On testing — and this is the transferable part — the C7 test asserts the invariant after exactly one load, which is a test of the FIX rather than of the SYSTEM. The industrial control is scenario/sequence testing that models the app's real call order: two loads back to back, launch-then-auth-ready, refresh-during-mutation. Where an invariant must hold over time rather than at an instant ('an emptied library is never silently reported as clean'), the tools are property-based testing over operation sequences and integration tests driven by the actual launch sequence, not unit assertions at the single moment the property is easiest to satisfy. Longer term, moving off a single JSON blob to SQLite/Core Data removes the whole-file-loss branch from the reachable state space.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — same defect as arui-2, verified in the same lines, and it correctly identifies the additional timing insult: `sendLink()` sets `showShareSheet = true` before any ack, so `UIActivityViewController` is presented over the copy and the caption underneath silently degrades from the honest gold hint to the reassuring default while the user is picking a recipient.
solutions.industrialSolution: As arui-2, with the sequencing point made explicit: the share flow must be a state machine with an ordered gate, not a fire-and-present. Model it as `enum ShareState { idle, saving, pendingUpload, ready(URL), failed(reason:retryable:) }`, drive the CTA off it with an exhaustive `switch`, and only reach `.ready` when the drop's own durable sync state is `clean` — sourced from `metadata.hasPendingWrites == false` or `waitForPendingWrites()`, Firestore's documented acknowledgement signals. Present `UIActivityViewController` only in `.ready`, or present it immediately with a `UIActivityItemProvider` that blocks on the ack and can refuse. Do not `dismiss()` the sheet on activity-sheet dismissal while the drop is still unresolved — the user needs to see the upload settle. And on a terminal failure the affordance must be recovery (retry / re-own / explain), not a link: shipping a link the app knows is dead is the failure mode the entire wave was commissioned to eliminate, and it is worse than an error because the sender confidently misinforms the recipient. Per-drop failure state (`[UUID: SyncFailure]` or, better, the per-record state from sync-1) is the prerequisite; a global `lastSyncError` can never be correct here because one drop's success is not evidence about another.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, including its platform premise — verified `launchCloudDelete`'s generic catch clears the tombstone at DropStore.swift:390-398 while `refresh`'s merge suppresses the cloud row only while the tombstone lives (:234), and Firestore's documented rules semantics make the stated rationale accurate but the remedy wrong: a delete of a never-uploaded document is evaluated with `resource == null`, so a rule written as `allow delete: if resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid` genuinely denies, which the code then treats as 'discharge the intent'.
solutions.industrialSolution: Fix the rule and the classification; the client workaround is treating a symptom. (1) RULES: the correct delete rule tolerates absence — `allow delete: if resource == null || resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid;` — which makes deleting a nonexistent document a harmless success and removes the entire denial case. Firestore's rules-conditions guide documents the `resource == null` idiom for exactly this. (2) CLASSIFY BEFORE DISCHARGING: only `.notFound` (or a confirmed delete) means the intent is satisfied. `.permissionDenied` means REFUSED — keep the tombstone so the merge keeps suppressing the row, move it to a durable `unresolvedDeleteIDs` set that `refresh` also honours, stop retrying it every reconcile, and surface it once. `.unavailable`/`.deadlineExceeded` means retry with exponential backoff. Blanket-clearing on any error is the defect. (3) BOUNDED RETRY + DEAD LETTER is the standard queue discipline: attempts counter, `nextAttemptAt`, and a terminal dead-letter state that is visible rather than logged — a log line is invisible on device and is not a user-facing failure surface. (4) STRUCTURALLY BEST: soft deletes. Most production Firestore apps delete by writing `deletedAt`/`isDeleted` via `update` rather than `delete`, because it avoids the exists/permission asymmetry entirely, gives server-side tombstones that all devices honour (a client-only tombstone that can be cleared is precisely how you get resurrection), and lets a Cloud Function or TTL policy do the physical delete with admin privileges. Firestore supports TTL policies natively for the reaping step.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — verified `reconcileCloud` at DropStore.swift:319-323 pushes only ids it can find in `drops` with no else-branch by design, the doc comment names `remove()` as the sole clearer, the set is rehydrated from UserDefaults at init (:211-212), and a row can leave `drops` permanently without passing through `remove()` via the resilient decode skip (:91-97) or the whole-file quarantine (:111), leaving an id that is never pushed, never cleared and never expires.
solutions.industrialSolution: This is the orphaned-outbox-entry problem, and it has one structural answer: THE OUTBOX ENTRY MUST CARRY ITS OWN PAYLOAD. A transactional-outbox row is self-sufficient — `{id, entityID, operation, payload, state, attempts, nextAttemptAt, lastError, createdAt}` — so it can always be retried no matter what happened to the entity table. A `Set<UUID>` in UserDefaults is a pointer-based outbox into a store that can lose the pointee, which is why an id can become both unpushable and unclearable. Storing the outbox in the SAME transactional store as the entity (Core Data/SwiftData/SQLite) additionally makes the entity's disappearance and its outbox entry's disappearance atomic, which is the definition of the pattern and removes the divergence at the source; UserDefaults is documented as a preferences store and can never be transactional with drops.json. Second, add the stuck-item recovery the offline-first literature prescribes: an explicit `inFlight(since:)` timestamp plus a reaper that re-queues or dead-letters entries past a threshold — modelling sync as binary worked/didn't is the documented cause of both infinite retry loops and silently lost data. Third, the UI rule the finding gets exactly right: the 'uploading' counter must be bounded by what the library can actually push. Anything unpushable is a DIFFERENT state ('1 drop couldn't be uploaded'), never progress — and after a load the store itself reports as clean, a pending id with no matching row is provably gone and should be reaped with a log, not carried forever.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED verbatim — verified ReactionService.swift:38-41 uses the no-completion `setData(from:)` so the surrounding catch can only observe a Codable encoding error, `send` is `async` but returns Void and reports nothing, and ReactionSession latches `sentEmoji` before awaiting the write; the rules premise is also documented — subcollection rules do NOT inherit from the parent, so `drops/{id}/reactions/{rid}` needs its own match block, and a rule keyed on the parent via `exists()` denies whenever the parent was never uploaded, which chains directly off sync-1.
solutions.industrialSolution: Three fixes. (1) ONE WRITE PATH. The proximate cause is that the acked-write continuation was implemented twice (FirebaseDropStore.swift:76-90, AccountService.swift:99-116) and omitted here — duplication guarantees drift. Extract a single `FirestoreWriter` (or a `DocumentReference` extension) that is the only way the app writes, and add a CI lint gate forbidding raw `setData(`/`updateData(` outside it. Note the modern SDK makes the helper nearly unnecessary: the async/await overloads (`try await ref.setData(...)`) are already ack-based, with the same documented property that they resume only on server commit. (2) OPTIMISTIC, BUT NOT UNCONFIRMED. Firestore's latency compensation is designed for exactly this UX — show the reaction instantly in a 'sending' style, and settle it when `snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites` flips false, with an explicit failure affordance and retry on rejection. The industry reference model is iMessage's Sent/Delivered distinction: optimistic rendering is fine, claiming delivery is not. Latch `sentEmoji` and start the 15-second wrap only after acknowledgement. (3) DECOUPLE THE WRITE FROM THE PARENT. A reaction is a fan-in write into another user's subtree; making it depend on the parent document existing means every unsynced drop silently kills the product's payoff loop. The industrial shape is either a callable Cloud Function (which can write with admin privileges and validate authorship) or a top-level `reactions` collection with `allow create: if request.auth != null && request.resource.data.uid == request.auth.uid`, indexed by dropId. For sender delivery, snapshot listeners are correct while foregrounded; FCM is the documented answer once the app is backgrounded.

crossCutting: THE SHARED DEFECT CLASS, precisely stated: truth about a PER-ENTITY outcome is stored in SHARED, EPHEMERAL, LAST-WRITER-WINS state. `lastSyncError`, `lastPersistError` and `localReadWarning` are single `String?` slots that any unrelated success nils; `pendingSyncIDs` is a bare `Set<UUID>` carrying no reason, no attempt count and no notion of permanence. Ten of the twenty findings are literally this one representational mistake (sync-1, sync-5, concurrency-1, arui-1, arui-2, arui-3, flows-3, flows-5, flows-6, and the derived-state variant in sync-2/flows-2). No amount of additional branching in the views can fix it, because the information the views would need was never durably recorded.

SECOND SHARED SHAPE — LEVELS WHERE THERE SHOULD BE EVENTS: a destructive or terminal outcome is recomputed from the most recent operation instead of being journaled. The quarantine warning is erased by the next load precisely BECAUSE the quarantine succeeded (sync-2/flows-2); `semanticMatteArmed` freezes because it is written inside a branch guarded by one of its own inputs (arui-4); an asset failure is announced into a handler that does not exist yet (arui-1). Incidents need durable records and explicit acknowledgement; only steady-state levels may be re-derived each pass.

THIRD SHARED SHAPE — READ-MODIFY-PUBLISH ACROSS AN AWAIT, with the pre-await snapshot winning (sync-3, sync-4, concurrency-2, concurrency-4, flows-1). Actor isolation eliminated the data races the previous wave fixed, and the team appears to have read that as eliminating races generally. It does not: Apple documents actor reentrancy explicitly (WWDC21 'Protect mutable state with Swift actors' — re-check assumptions after every await). Tellingly, the round-2 amendment applied meticulous generation guards to the WRITE pipeline and none at all to the READ path that actually publishes `drops`.

FOURTH SHARED SHAPE — ERRORS NOT CLASSIFIED BY PERMANENCE. Firestore hands you a complete taxonomy (`permissionDenied`, `unauthenticated`, `unavailable`, `deadlineExceeded`, `aborted`, `notFound`) and the app collapses all of it into `String?` plus a binary discharge decision. That collapse is what makes a refused delete indistinguishable from a completed one (flows-4) and a terminal owner mismatch indistinguishable from a healthy sync (sync-1/concurrency-1). Every failure needs exactly one of three dispositions: retry with backoff, escalate to the user as terminal, or mark resolved.

FIFTH SHARED SHAPE — THE TESTS CANNOT SEE THE BUGS, and this is why the same defect keeps returning one layer up each wave. The C7 test asserts the invariant after exactly one load, at the single instant it is easiest to satisfy (sync-2/flows-2). `StubCloudStore` is `@MainActor` with a non-suspending `save`, so from `@MainActor DropLibrary` no interleaving is possible in ANY test and the generation guards the wave was written for are structurally unexercised (concurrency-6) — which is the direct explanation for concurrency-3 surviving a green 59-test run. And the harness mutates the shipping app's UserDefaults keys (concurrency-5). The suite tests the fixes' happy paths, not the sequences in which the app actually runs.

THE UNIFYING OBSERVATION: every one of these is the PREVIOUSLY-FIXED BUG RE-CREATED ONE LAYER UP. SWE-3's dead link returns as sync-1/arui-2/flows-3; PBS-4's silent write returns as flows-6; SWE-8's vanishing drop returns as concurrency-4/flows-1; C7's silent empty library returns as sync-2/flows-2. That is the diagnostic signature of point-fixing symptoms while leaving the representation unchanged — the silence gets relocated, never removed. Three consecutive waves of this pattern is evidence about the method, not about the individual defects.

THE SINGLE INDUSTRIAL PRACTICE THAT WOULD PREVENT THE CLASS: make per-record sync state a DURABLE, EXPLICIT, EXHAUSTIVE STATE MACHINE stored transactionally alongside the record itself, and derive 100% of the UI from it — deleting every `@Published var lastXError: String?` and every `Set<UUID>` in UserDefaults. This is the transactional outbox pattern, the standard answer in offline-first mobile engineering. Concretely: one store (Core Data/SwiftData/SQLite — NOT drops.json plus UserDefaults, which cannot be written atomically across two stores) holding `{recordID, operation, payload, state ∈ {clean, pendingUpload, inFlight(since:), failedRetryable(attempts, nextAttemptAt), failedTerminal(reason), tombstoned}, updatedAt, lastError}`, with the outbox row written in the same transaction as the record and carrying its own payload so it can never be orphaned.

WHY THAT ONE CHANGE CLOSES ALL FIVE SHAPES AT ONCE: 'Synced' becomes a COMPUTATION over per-record states rather than a mutable slot, so no other drop's success and no successful read can clobber it (kills shape 1 — sync-1, sync-5, concurrency-1, flows-3, arui-2). Terminal failures and destructive events become durable rows that survive relaunch and clear only on acknowledgement (kills shape 2 — sync-2, flows-2). The outbox row carries its payload, so a lost entity row cannot immortalise a pending id and the pending counter is bounded by what is actually pushable (kills flows-5). Every error is classified into the state machine at ONE site using Firestore's error codes (kills shape 4 — flows-4, sync-1). And the exhaustive `switch` over the state enum makes the compiler REFUSE to let a new failure state fall through to a reassuring default — which is the specific mechanism that would have stopped the share sheet regressing to 'Sharing makes this drop visible to anyone with the link' for a drop the app knows is dead.

THE NECESSARY COMPANION PRACTICE (the reentrancy half, shape 3): one owner of the collection, fed by DIFFS rather than wholesale replacement. For a Firestore-backed app this is not a custom discipline but the documented architecture — a single `addSnapshotListener` bound to the auth lifecycle, applying `snapshot.documentChanges` (.added/.modified/.removed) into the store, with views observing published state. That deletes the three competing `.task` refresh triggers, deletes the pre-await snapshot assignment at DropStore.swift:244 that three separate reviewers independently flagged, and makes 'a delete undone by an in-flight read' unrepresentable rather than merely guarded. Where imperative reads must remain, epoch tokens plus `guard !Task.isCancelled` after every await are mandatory, since SwiftUI's `.task(id:)` cancellation is cooperative and the Firestore bridge ignores it entirely.

THE TESTING PRACTICE THAT MAKES IT STICK (shape 5): a test double must reproduce production's ISOLATION and its SUSPENSION POINTS, or it tests a program that does not exist. Make the fake cloud store an actor holding a controllable gate — a `CheckedContinuation` the test resumes explicitly — so a write can be parked mid-flight while the test deterministically drives a concurrent `remove`/`add`/`refresh` into the gap. That converts 'the generation guards are correct' from an untestable assertion into a deterministic test, and it is the only thing in this list that would have caught concurrency-3 before a human read the diff. Pair it with sequence-level tests that model the real launch order (launch refresh → auth-ready refresh → tab refresh) rather than single-operation assertions, injected `UserDefaults(suiteName:)` so no test can touch shipping state, and a warning-only `SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY = complete` CI lane ahead of the Swift 6 migration.

SEQUENCING RECOMMENDATION FOR THE OWNER: the twenty findings are roughly six defects. Fix the representation once (durable per-record sync state + outbox with payload) and sync-1, concurrency-1, sync-5, flows-5, arui-2 and flows-3 all close together. Fix the publish path once (listener + diffs, or epoch guard) and sync-4, concurrency-4 and flows-1 close together. Fix the write seam once (one acked-write helper + a lint gate) and flows-6 closes with a guarantee it stays closed. The remaining independent items are sync-2/flows-2 (durable quarantine record), flows-4 (rules fix + error classification), concurrency-2 (server-side seeding), arui-1 (build-time asset validation + render-time asset state), arui-4 (reconciler at the transition sites), and the test-harness pair concurrency-5/concurrency-6 — which should be done FIRST, because without them the next wave's fixes will be just as unverifiable as this one's.
